source_caption:
To completely submerge the audience in the profoundly terrifying, intensely confusing subjective reality of John Nash’s schizophrenia, director Ron Howard made a wildly brilliant, deeply controversial creative departure from historical fact. While the real-life mathematical genius almost exclusively suffered from auditory hallucinations, Howard and screenwriter Akiva Goldsman chose to manifest his delusions as fiercely vivid, completely physical human beings. By brilliantly hiding this devastating truth in plain sight and allowing the audience to completely believe these characters were real until the film’s massively heartbreaking second half, Howard masterfully proves that the most viscerally powerful cinematic empathy is sometimes achieved by deliberately rewriting reality to force the viewer to question their own very eyes.
⠀
A Beautiful Mind (2001), directed by Ron Howard, starring Russell Crowe, Jennifer Connelly, Ed Harris. A fiercely brilliant, deeply introverted mathematical genius completely revolutionizes the field of economics, only to profoundly spiral into a terrifying, violently paranoid battle with severe schizophrenia, relying heavily on the fiercely unwavering love of his dedicated wife to desperately claw his way back to reality and ultimately claim the Nobel Prize.

source_details.title: A Beautiful Mind
source_details.synopsis: A Beautiful Mind is a 2001 American biographical drama film about the mathematician John Nash who won a Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. Nash's character was played by actor Russell Crowe. The film was directed by Ron Howard and based on a screenplay by Akiva Goldsman, who adapted the 1998 biography by Sylvia Nasar. In addition to Crowe, the film's cast features Ed Harris, Jennifer Connelly, Paul Bettany, Adam Goldberg, Judd Hirsch, Josh Lucas, Anthony Rapp, and Christopher Plummer in supporting roles.
